description: Forms lesions on aerial parts such as leaves, panicles, panicle branches, nodes and grains; the most common forms are leaf, panicle and panicle-branch blast
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

description: Attacks all aerial parts including leaves, leaf collar, nodes, neck and parts of the panicle, and sometimes the leaf sheath
short_quote: "all above ground parts of a rice plant"
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

description: Leaf lesions are spindle-shaped. In the chronic type the margin is red; in the acute type fine gray mold (conidia) covers the lesion surface
growth_stage: Not stated (paddy field from late June; see timing row)
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

description: Early lesions are white to gray-green spots with dark green borders
short_quote: "white to gray-green lesions or spots, with dark green borders"
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

description: Older lesions are elliptical to spindle-shaped, with white to gray centers and red to brown or necrotic borders. Some are diamond-shaped, wide in the middle and pointed at both ends. As lesions enlarge and merge, the whole leaf dies
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

description: Leaf spots start as small white, gray or bluish specks. Under humid conditions they enlarge quickly into elliptical or diamond-shaped spots or linear lesions pointed at both ends, with gray to white centers and narrow brown borders. In severe cases leaves and whole plants die
short_quote: "white, gray or blue-tinged spots"
growth_stage: Seedling to late tillering (leaf blast phase)
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

description: Spindle-shaped leaf spots with brown or reddish-brown to yellowish-brown borders, ashy centers and pointed ends. Fully developed lesions are usually 1.0–1.5 cm long and 0.3–0.5 cm wide. Symptoms vary with growth stage, cultivar susceptibility and environment
short_quote: "1.0 -1.5 cm in length and 0.3 -0.5cm in breadth"
source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

description: Leaf blast lesions are usually elongated with pointed ends. Brown spot lesions are rounder, brown, and surrounded by a yellow halo
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)
location_in_source: "How to identify" comparison paragraph below the photo

description: With severe leaf blast the whole hill turns reddish and stops growing (stunting, "jwaji")
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

description: Leaf blast can kill plants from the seedling to the tillering stage
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

description: The leaf collar becomes discolored like neck symptoms, and the attached leaf blade also discolors and dies
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

description: The IRRI leaf/collar fact sheet only shows a "Collar blast" photo and does not describe collar lesions in text
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

description: Dark-brown lesions form on nodes, which break easily; under high humidity the surface is covered with gray mold
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice panicle blast (NCPMS-Panicle blast; text identical to the leaf blast page)

description: Node infection appears as bands, with black to gray-brown lesions. Infected nodes can cause the culm supporting the panicle to break
short_quote: "Node infection occurs in banded pattern."
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (node and neck)" (IRRI-Node/neck blast)

description: Infected nodes discolor and shrivel, and plants often lodge
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

description: Infected nodes turn black and rot
source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

description: The neck and panicle branches dry out light brown, and under humid conditions gray mold appears on the surface
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice panicle blast (NCPMS-Panicle blast; text identical to the leaf blast page)

description: Neck lesions are gray-brown and girdle the neck, causing the neck and panicle to fall over. Node blast and neck blast often occur together and look similar
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (node and neck)" (IRRI-Node/neck blast)
location_in_source: "What it does" paragraph 2; "How to identify" bullet 4

description: Rotten-neck symptoms start at the node at the base of the panicle. Tissue browns and shrivels, so the stem breaks and lodges. If the panicle does not drop it turns white to gray, or unfilled florets turn gray
short_quote: "Rotten neck symptoms appear at the base of the panicle"
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

description: Infection at the panicle base causes rotten neck and the panicle drops
source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

description: Panicles affected by panicle blast become empty (unfilled)
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice panicle blast (NCPMS-Panicle blast; text identical to the leaf blast page)

description: If the neck is infected before the milk stage, no grain forms; infection afterwards produces poor-quality grain. Node and neck blast produce whiteheads like stem borers. Stem-borer whiteheads pull out easily, but blast whiteheads do not
short_quote: "tugging on the stem will not result in removal"
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (node and neck)" (IRRI-Node/neck blast)
location_in_source: "How to identify" bullet 5 and lower bullets

description: Gray-brown lesions form at the branching joints of panicle branches and floret stalks
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

description: In severe cases secondary panicle branches and grains are also attacked, producing partly filled grains ('whiteheads')
source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

description: Acute-type leaf lesions; under high humidity gray mold (conidia) appears on the surface of the neck, panicle branches and nodes
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

description: The pathogen spreads by spores carried by wind and rain (Figure 1 spore photo)
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

description: Because of seed-borne inoculum, leaf lesions also form in the nursery. In the paddy field it occurs mainly from late June and leads on to panicle blast. Panicle blast infection occurs around heading, and the main inoculum is thought to be leaf-blast lesions on the upper leaves
growth_stage: Seedling raising; paddy field from late June; around heading
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

description: Occurs at all growth stages, but leaf blast declines once plants mature and acquire adult-plant resistance
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, "Blast (leaf and collar)" (IRRI-Leaf/collar blast)

description: Found from seedling to maturity. The leaf blast phase is seedling to late tillering, and neck blast occurs at heading (US basis)
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3153 "Blast of Rice" (Groth & Hollier, 6/10) (LSU-Blast)

description: Severe in years with frequent rain and low summer temperatures during the growing season, especially with cold damage. Frequent rain and gloomy, humid weather around heading cause major panicle blast outbreaks. Heavy nitrogen application makes it worse
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

description: Occurrence increases with low night temperatures (17–20 °C), high humidity, excess nitrogen, foggy and cloudy weather, and dense planting
source_name: Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture, Rice Research & Development Institute, Rice blast page (DOA-SriLanka)

description: Belongs to the ascomycetes (perfect state), but the conidial state is usual in the field. Conidia are colorless, pear-shaped, with 2 septa, 14–37 × 5–12 µm. On media it forms dark-brown globose perithecia and spindle-shaped ascospores
short_quote: "conidia are colorless, pear-shaped, with two septa" (translated from Korean)
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

description: Genus *Pyricularia* characters: conidia are solitary, pyriform to obclavate, narrowing toward the tip with a rounded base, 2-septate, colorless to pale brown, with a distinct basal hilum. Conidiophores are brown and grow sympodially, and conidia detach rhexolytically. Ascospores are colorless, fusiform, curved, with 3 transverse septa
short_quote: "pyriform to obclavate, narrowed toward tip, rounded at the base, 2-septate"
source_name: Klaubauf S. et al. 2014. Studies in Mycology 79:85–120, "Pyriculariaceae" phylogenetic paper (Klaubauf 2014)

description: The *P. oryzae* Cavara entry in the same paper gives only a list of examined specimens and a figure (Fig. 15: sporulation on barley seed on SNA, conidiophores and conidia, scale bar 10 µm) and no conidial size figures (Unconfirmed). Its specimen list includes isolates from weeds and grasses (*Festuca*, *Lolium*, *Phleum*, *Panicum miliaceum*) in Suwon and Yongin, Korea
source_name: Klaubauf S. et al. 2014. Studies in Mycology 79:85–120, "Pyriculariaceae" phylogenetic paper (Klaubauf 2014)

description: The pathogen grows at 8–37 °C with an optimum of 25–28 °C. Conidia form at 12–34 °C, and the optimum for sporulation is the same as for growth
source_name: RDA National Crop Pest Management System, paddy rice leaf blast (NCPMS-Leaf blast)

description: Initially, water-soaked oval lesions that look blanched form on the leaf sheath; they enlarge as dark green lesions and the surrounding area turns light brown. Lesion size is not uniform
short_quote: "water-soaked oval lesions, as if blanched" (translated from Korean)
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)

description: Oval to oblong gray-green lesions form on the leaf sheath, usually 1–3 cm long. In flooded fields they first appear just above the soil or water surface
short_quote: "usually 1-3 cm long, on the leaf sheath"

description: Large oval spots form on the leaf sheath. Lesions about 0.5–1 cm wide and 1–3 cm long form slightly above the water line on infected stems. Lesion centers are grayish-white or light green, with brown to reddish-brown borders
short_quote: "about 0.5 - 1 cm in width and 1 - 3 cm in length"
growth_stage: Infection begins from late tillering to internode elongation
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

description: Starts as small water-soaked oval or irregular lesions near the water line on lower leaf sheaths, light green or gray in color. Lesions enlarge and merge into large irregular blotches girdling the sheath. Old lesions have tan to light-brown centers with distinct dark green or brown borders
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)
location_in_source: "Symptoms" Initial Symptoms and Lesion Development bullets (Fig. 3A–C)

description: Leaf lesions are usually irregular; with age the center becomes grayish-white and the margin brown

Irregular spots form on the leaf blade. When sheath lesions merge, the leaf blade turns yellow-orange and eventually dies. The LSU photo gallery describes leaf lesions as 'snakeskin-like' (gallery caption text Unconfirmed; seen only in a search snippet)
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

description: In highly susceptible cultivars the fungus spreads into the culm from early sheath infection. Infected culms weaken and tillers lodge or collapse
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

description: Infected leaves senesce and die quickly, and young tillers also die. As a result canopy leaf area falls and yield declines
Severely affected plants show early leaf senescence, fewer tillers and poor grain filling
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

description: As the rice grows, lesions gradually move upward. Secondary spread happens when mycelium from sheath lesions forms new lesions on neighboring stems, hills and leaves
plant_part: Leaf sheath to leaves and adjacent hills
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)

description: Under favorable conditions early lesions multiply and enlarge, moving up the sheath and onto the leaves. They then spread to tillers of neighboring hills (transplanted) or neighboring plants (direct-seeded)
plant_part: Leaf sheath to leaves to adjacent hills

description: Lower leaf sheaths and blades are attacked at internode elongation. After panicle emergence, disease progresses quickly up to the flag leaf in susceptible cultivars. The fungus does not form spores and spreads by growing from hill to hill, so it appears as circular patches in the field
short_quote: "Infected plants are usually found in a circular pattern"
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

description: The disease progresses in two phases. In the vertical phase, sclerotia or debris infect the tiller base at the water line and move up into the canopy; in the horizontal phase, mycelium spreads hill to hill by physical contact with healthy tissue. In severe cases stems weaken and lodge early. Cultivar susceptibility increases after heading
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

description: Sclerotia are mycelial masses of irregular size and shape, but most are brown and round, about 1–2 mm. The fungus overwinters as sclerotia, which attach to leaf sheaths after transplanting and cause disease
short_quote: "mostly brown, round, about 1-2 mm" (translated from Korean)
growth_stage: Formed late July to early August
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)
location_in_source: Pathogen information > pathogen characteristics; symptom description sentence 2

description: Sclerotia are white at first and turn brown to black as they mature. They can be 6 mm or more in diameter and float when fields are flooded. They survive in soil for more than 2 years. Laboratory formation stages are (A) white mycelial tangle → (B) differentiation to yellow-light brown → (C) brown, with visible droplets → (D) black, dry mature sclerotium
short_quote: "They can be 6 mm or more in diameter"
growth_stage: Late disease development, end of season
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

description: Under high humidity, cottony white mycelium is often seen on the surface of infected sheaths
short_quote: "Cottony white fungal mycelium"
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

description: Sclerotia are tightly interwoven mycelial masses covered by an impermeable, hydrophobic layer secreted by the fungus. They form on lesion surfaces of weedy grasses, rice and soybean
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

description: In subtropical environments disease is mainly started by sclerotia, and diseased crops produce up to 2 million sclerotia per m². The role of sclerotia in the tropics is uncertain. The fungus does not produce airborne spores and spreads by mycelium growing over plant tissue
short_quote: "does not produce aerially dispersed spores"

description: Resembles stem rot and stem-borer damage. Confirm by irregular sheath lesions (water-soaked to gray-green early, grayish-white with brown border later) and the presence of sclerotia
Overwintering sclerotia float to the water surface during puddling and attach between leaves and sheaths after transplanting. Most sclerotia form from late July to early August
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)
location_in_source: Disease environment sentence 1; symptom description sentence 2

description: Symptoms are usually observed from tillering to the milk stage
short_quote: "from tillering to milk stage"

description: Infection usually begins from late tillering to internode elongation
source_name: LSU AgCenter Pub. 3123 "Sheath Blight of Rice" (2 pages) (LSU-SB)

description: Infection can occur at any growth stage but is most common after tillering. Symptoms appear from tillering to booting and progress quickly under hot, humid conditions
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

description: Infection is possible at 22–35 °C, optimum 30–32 °C. Disease is heavy when humidity between hills stays at 96% or above. Excess nitrogen, dense planting, cropping season and cultivar affect it
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Sheath blight (NCPMS-Sheath blight)

description: Occurs with high temperature (28–32 °C), high nitrogen fertilization and canopy relative humidity of 85–100%. More prevalent in the rainy season
Favored by 73–95 °F (about 22.8–35 °C), optimum 86–90 °F (about 30–32.2 °C), and relative humidity above 95%
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

description: Under the microscope the hyphae consist of long multinucleate cells with septa. They branch at 90° from the main hypha with a constriction at the branch point and a septum just above the branch. Hyphae are colorless. Sexual spores are produced but rarely observed in Arkansas fields
short_quote: "branching at 90° angles to the main hyphae with constriction"
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

description: The causal agent is *R. solani* AG1-IA. An AG (anastomosis group) is defined by the ability of genetically similar isolates to fuse hyphae and is used for identification. AG11 and AG4 cause seedling damping-off but not sheath blight
source_name: University of Arkansas FSA7583 "Rice Sheath Blight" (Nicolli, Dalla Lana, Pedrozo, Ronning; PDF dated 2025-08) (UAEX-SB)

description: 2,276 *R. solani* isolates from 68 crops in Korea were divided by anastomosis testing into AG-1 (1,091 isolates), AG-2-1, AG-2-2, AG-3, AG-4 and AG-5. Of AG-1, 791 isolates were cultural type IA, and IA was isolated from 7 crops. The optimum mycelial growth temperature of AG-1 is 26–30 °C, and the minimum for AG-1 (IA) is 10–11 °C. At 26 °C, AG-1 (IA) and (IB) grew fastest after AG-1 (IC). The abstract does not name the 7 crops yielding IA, so whether rice isolates were IA cannot be confirmed from this abstract alone (Unconfirmed)
source_name: Kim W.G., Cho W.D., Lee Y.H. 1994. Korean Journal of Mycology 22(4):309–324, "Anastomosis Groups and Cultural Characteristics of *Rhizoctonia solani* Isolates from Crops in Korea" (Kim 1994)

description: Early lesions have a dark-brown oval necrotic area surrounded by a yellow toxic zone (halo). Over time they become large round lesions with concentric rings
short_quote: "yellow toxic zone around dark-brown oval necrotic area" (translated from Korean)
growth_stage: Not stated (lower leaves more prone to infection)
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: Leaf lesions appear from tillering. At first they are small, round, dark-brown to purple-brown spots
Fully developed lesions are round to oval with light-brown to gray centers and reddish-brown borders. IRRI states that the reddish-brown border is caused by a toxin produced by the fungus
short_quote: "reddish brown margin caused by the toxin"

description: On susceptible cultivars lesions are 5–14 mm long and leaves may wilt. On resistant cultivars lesions are brown and pinhead-sized
short_quote: "On resistant varieties, the lesions are brown and pinhead-sized."

description: On some cultivars it can be mistaken for blast lesions. Confirm by round brown spots with gray centers surrounded by reddish-brown borders
The most conspicuous damage is the many large spots on leaves, which can kill the whole leaf

Infected seedlings develop small, round, yellow-brown or brown lesions. Lesions can girdle the coleoptile and distort the first and second leaves. Heavily infected seed causes seedling blight, killing 10–58% of seedlings
location_in_source: "How to identify" first bullet; "Why is it important"

description: Stems basically show fine dark-brown markings. Later these enlarge and merge so the whole stem turns pale brown. Panicle stalks develop dark-brown streaks and later turn entirely dark brown
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: Leaf sheath lesions resemble leaf lesions
location_in_source: "How to identify" paragraph below the photo

description: Grains develop dark-brown spots that later become grayish-white collapsed areas. Often the whole grain surface browns. Unlike blast, it does not attack quickly from the panicle tip and does not cause whiteheads
short_quote: "does not cause whiteheads as blast does" (translated from Korean)
growth_stage: Grains are more prone to infection the closer to heading
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: Infected glumes and panicle branches show dark-brown to black oval spots or discoloration of the whole surface. Infected florets fill incompletely and quality falls. The fungus penetrates grains, producing spotted, discolored grain ('pecky rice'). Seed infection produces unfilled or spotted, discolored seed
location_in_source: "How to identify" 2 paragraphs below the photo; "What it does"

description: In September 2023, brown spot lesions appeared on leaves, necks and panicles of rice in Gimje and Gunsan, Jeonbuk, and were collected intensively. Isolates were also obtained from leaf lesions in Jangheung (Jeonnam), Sancheong, Sacheon and Goseong (Gyeongnam) and Gyeongju (Gyeongbuk), and in 2024 two isolates came from leaves in Suncheon, Jeonnam (collected in July and August)
source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)

description: On secondary signs: the NCPMS original says lesions do not form conidia, and that healthy tissue around the lesion dies and forms conidia from the start. The meaning of the sentence is ambiguous, so it is kept as in the original
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: Disease occurs throughout the growing period but rises sharply in the paddy field after panicle initiation. Lower leaves are more prone, and grains are more prone closer to heading. Stems, panicles, panicle stalks and panicle branches become more prone as days after heading increase. The last panicle infection affecting yield is up to 25 days after heading. Conidia trapped 80 cm above ground are few from booting to the dough stage and increase sharply near harvest
short_quote: "last panicle infection affecting yield is up to 25 days after heading" (translated from Korean)
growth_stage: From panicle initiation to 25 days after heading
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: Can occur at all growth stages, but infection from maximum tillering to grain filling is most important. Infection requires 8–24 hours of leaf wetness and occurs at 86–100% RH and 16–36 °C
short_quote: "most critical during maximum tillering up to the ripening stages"

description: In Korea brown spot normally occurs at harvest, but interest has grown because its timing has recently shifted. Incidence in 2001–2008 was 30–50% (introduction; original source in the paper's references)
source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)

description: Optimum temperature for conidial germination is 20–30 °C, with 90% germinating in 3 hours. Infection needs air humidity of 70% at flowering and 90% at the dough stage. Unlike the blast fungus, conidia rarely fly at night; they fly mostly from 08–09 h to 15 h, and field spore counts peak near maturity
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: Conidia are nearly cylindrical, usually curved, pale brown to yellow-brown, with 6–14 septa, 63–153 µm long and 14–22 µm wide. They germinate from one or both end cells. Conidiophores are septate, about 600 µm long and 4–8 µm wide
short_quote: "has 6-14 septa and is 63-153 µm long" (translated from Korean)
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: The original says the 'ascus' is dark brown, globose to elliptical, 360–780 µm in diameter. It then again says the 'ascus' is clavate to cylindrical-clavate, 21–26 µm wide and 140–235 µm long. Ascospores are 235–648 µm long and 4–9 µm wide, filiform with 8–12 septa and a mucilaginous sheath, coiled helically within the ascus
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: For 6 representative Korean isolates (14 days on PDA), conidia ranged 27.4–96.3 µm long and 6.0–19.8 µm wide. Isolate means ranged from 53.1 × 11.2 µm (F1305) to 75.0 × 15.2 µm (F1371), based on at least 2 experiments per isolate and 50 measurements per experiment. In slide culture, 2–4 conidia were borne per conidiophore. Septum numbers were not reported (Unconfirmed)
source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)
location_in_source: Results mycological traits paragraph; Table 3 and footnotes

description: At 25 °C on PDA all isolates grew fast, forming cottony colonies 45–70 mm in diameter in 90 mm Petri dishes within 5 days. The upper side mostly has a gray cottony center, with white margins in some isolates (F1253, F1371). The reverse is dark gray to almost black
source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)

description: ITS sequences of all 50 isolates were identical and matched *B. oryzae* CBS 199.54 at 100% (562/562 bp). RAPD divided them into 5 groups (group A 84%). Lesions were observed 1 day after inoculation (30 °C, 80–90% humidity) (seedling inoculation conditions)
source_name: Kim S., Chung H., Jang S.-H. et al. 2025. Plant Pathology Journal 41(5):671–681, doi 10.5423/PPJ.FT.08.2025.0106, RAPD and mycological traits of 50 Korean *B. oryzae* isolates (Kim 2025)
location_in_source: Methods pathogenicity test; Results ITS paragraph

description: Produces the non-host-specific toxin ophiobolin
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Brown spot (NCPMS-Brown spot)

description: Paddy-field symptoms after peak tillering start on mature lower leaves. In the original wording, small water-soaked lesions form on 'the leaf margin 5–6 cm below the leaf blade' (whether the reference point is the leaf tip is unclear in the original)
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: Lesions usually enlarge after 2–3 days, turning yellow to yellow-orange and spreading up and down as well as widening. The boundary with healthy tissue is water-soaked. They start from one or both leaf margins and spread to the leaf center, forming wavy-edged lesions. Over time they fade from yellowish-white to white or grayish-white and become dirty-colored due to secondary colonizers
short_quote: "enlarges into wavy-edged lesions" (translated from Korean)
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: On mature plants it usually appears as water-soaked to yellow-orange stripes on the leaf blade, leaf tip or mechanical wounds. Lesion margins are wavy and progress toward the leaf base
short_quote: "Lesions have a wavy margin and progress toward the leaf base."
location_in_source: "How to identify" Check for lesions, first bullet

description: Old lesions turn yellow to grayish-white, and black dots appear as various saprophytes grow. On severely affected leaves lesions can extend to the leaf sheath
location_in_source: "How to identify" paragraph below the ooze photo

description: Appears as light green to gray-green water-soaked stripes near the tips and margins of young plants after transplanting. Later lesions merge into yellowish-white with wavy margins, and eventually the whole leaf turns white or gray and dies
short_quote: "pale-green to grey-green water-soaked streaks near the leaf tip and margins"
growth_stage: Young plants after transplanting to late stage
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

description: Symptoms appear mainly on leaf blades and leaf sheaths
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: In more susceptible cultivars, leaf sheaths and culms can also be attacked
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

description: Symptoms sometimes also appear on grains
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: Gray to light-brown lesions can form on the glumes of the panicle, which can lead to sterility or reduced grain quality
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

description: Infection at booting does not affect yield but lowers grain quality and increases the proportion of broken grains

Late in the nursery, small water-soaked lesions appear on lower leaves, and dried beads of bacterial exudate form on the surface. A few days later they turn yellow, dry white from the tip, and the leaf dies rapidly
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: From about 20–30 days after transplanting until peak tillering, seedlings suddenly dry up and die. There are no distinct symptoms, but beads smaller than millet grains are visible on leaf margins or tips. This does not occur after peak tillering. It is a wilt caused by the pathogen multiplying at the base and blocking the vessels
short_quote: "characteristically does not occur after peak tillering" (translated from Korean)
growth_stage: 20-30 days after transplanting to peak tillering
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: In seedlings, infected leaves turn gray-green and roll. As the disease progresses, leaves turn yellow to straw-colored and wilt, and the whole seedling dries and dies

Systemic infection ('kresek') occurs in young plants or tillering plants of highly susceptible cultivars, causing leaves to dry, wilt and die. It is particularly severe in young transplanted plants. Larger plants may have leaves that yellow, wilt and die, and surviving plants are yellow and stunted. Clipping leaves at transplanting is an effective route for kresek spread (pale yellow leaves, severe wilting, frequent death)
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

description: When morning dew forms, pale milky dew droplets appear on the lesion surface and dry into yellow beads. These beads fall onto the water surface with wind and become secondary inoculum
short_quote: "pale milky dew forms and dries into yellow beads" (translated from Korean)
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: On young lesions, bacterial ooze resembling milky dew drops is visible in the early morning. The ooze later dries into small yellow beads on the underside of the leaf
short_quote: "bacterial ooze resembling a milky dew drop"
location_in_source: "How to identify" Check for lesions, bullet 2

description: Bacterial ooze may be seen on water-soaked stripes in the early morning. Multiplied bacteria are exuded as slimy droplets and re-enter through hydathodes
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

description: To tell kresek from stem-borer damage, squeeze the lower part of an infected seedling between the fingers. With kresek, yellow bacterial ooze comes out of the cut surface, and unlike stem-borer-damaged plants it does not pull out easily. For leaves, cut across a young lesion, place it in a clear container of clean water, and after a few minutes hold it to the light to see whether turbid liquid streams from the cut end
location_in_source: "How to identify" kresek paragraph, last "To quickly diagnose" bullet

description: Usually develops around heading, but in chronic and heavily affected areas it develops early in the paddy field and rarely even in the nursery. The number of rainy days and rainfall from late July to late August are important. Major outbreaks occur with July mean temperature 22–24 °C, July rainfall of 200 mm or more and wind speed of 15 m/s or more; incidence was 8.8% after 12 hours of submergence and 72.7% after 48 hours
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: In temperate regions it is usually observed late in the nursery (citing Ou 1985). In both temperate and tropical regions, 25–34 °C, RH above 70%, strong winds and frequent heavy rain (typhoons) favor disease (citing Mew et al. 1993)
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

description: Occurs readily at 25–34 °C and RH above 70%. It spreads by ooze droplets during strong winds and continuous heavy rain. The earlier it occurs, the greater the yield loss
location_in_source: "Why and where it occurs"; "Why is it important"

description: A bacterial vascular disease. Cells are rods 1–2 × 0.8 µm with rounded ends and a single terminal flagellum. The original gives the flagellum as '30μ thick and 8.75μ long' (units as written). Gram-negative, no spores. The surface is covered by sticky polysaccharide slime (capsule)
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: Aerobic, motile, Gram-negative rod. Non-spore-forming and capsulated, occurring singly or in pairs, 1.1–2.0 × 0.4–0.6 µm, with one polar flagellum. It mainly attacks vascular tissue. By contrast, pv. *oryzicola* (bacterial leaf streak) attacks mesophyll parenchyma
short_quote: "1.1-2.0 x 0.4-0.6 µm in size, with one polar flagellum"
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)
location_in_source: DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION > Morphology; BIOLOGY sentence 1

description: Grows relatively slowly, but forms yellow, round, smooth colonies on nutrient media in 3–4 days. It can grow even at 5–10 °C, with an optimum of 26–30 °C. Without nutrients it survives about 20 days at 20 °C and a few days at 30 °C. It survives 8 months or more in diseased straw and on *Leersia* grass and similar hosts
source_name: NCPMS paddy rice Bacterial blight (NCPMS-Bacterial blight)

description: Isolated on PSA, NBY, GF agar or semi-selective media. After 3–7 days on NA, colonies are round, entire, smooth, convex, opaque and pale yellow to straw yellow (1–2 mm). Optimum growth temperature is 25–30 °C, and it does not survive long on solid media. Catalase positive and unable to reduce nitrate
short_quote: "pale to straw yellow,1-2 mm in size"
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)
location_in_source: Morphology sentences 2-5; Detection and identification methods first sentence

description: Enters mainly through hydathodes at leaf tips and margins, and also through stomata and wounds. After multiplying in the epithem it moves into the xylem and travels both up and down within the vessels
plant_part: Leaf tip and margins to xylem vessels
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzae* datasheet (BIOLOGY 2022-06-03, DETECTION AND IDENTIFICATION 2022-06-16) (EPPO-XANTOR)

description: Water-soaked to yellow-orange stripes form on the leaf blade, leaf tip or mechanical wounds. Margins are wavy and progress toward the leaf base. In the early morning, slime resembling milky dew forms on young lesions and dries into small yellow beads on the leaf underside.
short_quote: "Lesions have a wavy margin and progress toward the leaf base."

description: After peak tillering, small water-soaked lesions form on the leaf margin 5–6 cm below the blade tip. Pale milky dew forms during morning dew and dries into yellow beads. After 2–3 days lesions spread up and down as yellow to yellow-orange areas, forming wavy-edged lesions. Over time they change from yellowish-white to white or grayish-white.
short_quote: "enlarges into wavy-edged lesions" (translated from Korean)

description: Early symptoms are narrow, dark green, water-soaked streaks of variable length between the veins, initially only on the leaf blade. As lesions enlarge they develop yellow halos, turn yellow-orange to brown depending on cultivar, and may merge.
short_quote: "narrow, dark-green, water-soaked, interveinal streaks of various lengths"
source_name: EPPO Global Database, *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzicola* (XANTTO) Datasheet

description: Bacterial exudate is commonly seen on the streaks, as tiny amber droplets.
short_quote: "tiny amber-coloured drops"

description: In severe infections yellow-orange (amber) exudate emerges from stomata as small droplets. When dry, the exudate becomes small sticky beads (stalked or not). It may also dry into threads, which can be spread by dry wind.
short_quote: "sticky tiny beads with or without small stalks"

description: At advanced stages it is hard to distinguish from bacterial blight (Xoo). However, Xoc lesion margins stay straight while Xoo lesions are wavy. The two pathovars occur together in the same field and sometimes on the same plant.
short_quote: "lesion margins remain linear (rather than wavy…)"

description: In the final stage the streaks turn brown to gray and leaves may dry completely and die.
Infected florets turn brown or black, and the ovary and stamens die. Symptomatic infected seeds have browned glumes and necrotic endosperm.
short_quote: "browning of glumes and necrotic endosperm"

description: Often occurs together with feeding injury by leaf-folder larvae such as *Cnaphalocrocis medinalis* or the rice hispa (*Dicladispa armigera*), because feeding wounds let bacteria enter easily.

Enters mainly through stomata or wounds (insects, heavy rain, wind). It multiplies between mesophyll parenchyma cells (apoplast) and spreads along intercellular spaces without entering the vascular bundles. Xoo, in contrast, enters mainly through hydathodes and multiplies in the vascular bundles. This difference underlies the difference in lesion shape.
short_quote: "without entering the vascular tissues"

description: Aerobic, motile, Gram-negative rod. Non-spore-forming and capsulated, occurring singly or in pairs, 1.0–2.5 × 0.4–0.6 µm, with one polar flagellum.
short_quote: "1.0-2.5 x 0.4-0.6 µm in size, with one polar flagellum"

description: Colonies after 3 days on NA are round with smooth margins, smooth, convex and opaque, pale yellow to straw yellow, 1–2 mm. Optimum growth 25–30 °C. Because it grows slowly it is easily overgrown by fast-growing contaminants such as *Pantoea*. PSA, NBY and GF media are used for isolation, and XOS is a semi-selective medium for seed detection.
short_quote: "pale to straw yellow, 1-2 mm in size"

description: Early symptoms are small water-soaked linear lesions between the veins, initially dark green and later light brown to yellowish-gray.
short_quote: "small, water-soaked, linear lesions between leaf veins"
source_name: IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank, Bacterial leaf streak
location_in_source: How to identify, "Check for lesions" item 1

description: Lesions are translucent when held against the light. In very severe cases the whole leaf browns and dies.
short_quote: "translucent when held against the light"

description: Under humid conditions yellow droplets of bacterial exudate are visible on the leaf surface, containing masses of bacterial cells.
short_quote: "yellow droplets of bacterial ooze"

description: If the advancing part of a streak is cut and placed in a glass of water, bacterial masses stream out and the water usually becomes turbid after 5 minutes.
short_quote: "makes the water turbid after five minutes"
location_in_source: How to identify, paragraph under "To confirm"

description: It can be confused with narrow brown spot. Leaf streak lesions are usually narrower; narrow brown spot lesions are not translucent and have no bacterial exudate.
short_quote: "narrow brown spot lesions are not translucent"

description: In early infection, especially when lesions of both diseases are on the same leaf, bacterial blight and leaf streak look identical. Biochemical, pathogenicity and serological tests are needed to distinguish them.
short_quote: "Blight and streak symptoms look the same at the early stage"

description: Infection occurs at early stages from maximum tillering to panicle initiation. Mature plants recover easily, so yield loss is small. It occurs in hot, humid areas and carries over to the next crop through seed and infected stubble.
short_quote: "from maximum tillering to panicle initiation"
location_in_source: Why and where it occurs, paragraphs 2 and 4

description: Infected plants have leaves that brown and dry. In severe cases the photosynthetic area falls and grain weight decreases.
From tillering to booting, small dark green water-soaked streaks form between veins. The streaks are confined by veins and grow only lengthwise, soon turning yellow or orange-brown.
short_quote: "longitudinal, limited by the veins"
source_name: TNAU Agritech Portal, Paddy expert system: Bacterial leaf streak

description: Bacterial exudate is visible along the whole streak as small yellow or amber droplets.
short_quote: "tiny yellow or amber colored droplets"

description: Streaks merge into large blotches and can cover the whole leaf. In severe cases lesions turn brown to grayish-white and dry out.
Infected florets and seeds discolor brown or black, the ovary, stamens and endosperm die, and glumes brown.

Rod-shaped, without spores or capsule (EPPO says "capsulated"). One polar flagellum, Gram-negative, aerobic, grows well at 28 °C. Colonies on NA are pale yellow, round, smooth, convex, viscous and with smooth margins.
short_quote: "pale yellow, circular, smooth, convex, and viscid"

description: Narrow dark green water-soaked streaks of variable length form between the veins of the leaf blade. As lesions enlarge they turn yellow-orange to brown, and amber bacterial exudate is visible. It is hard to distinguish from bacterial blight; the main late-stage difference is the lesion margin shape (straight in leaf streak, wavy in bacterial blight).
short_quote: "straight in leaf streak and wavy in leaf blight"
source_name: Oregon State Univ. Plant Clinic (S. B. Jepson), "Bacterial leaf streak of rice" 1-page sheet (stated as reprinted from CABI Crop Protection Compendium 2005)

description: Enters through stomata and surface wounds (usually from insects), and bacterial masses develop in the parenchyma.
short_quote: "Masses of bacteria develop in the parenchyma."

description: In Madagascar rice fields (both upland and lowland rice, 30–80% of plants affected), water-soaked lesions developed into translucent yellow streaks with exudate visible on the surface. On inoculated leaves, water-soaked lesions with yellow exudate were reproduced after about 7 days.
short_quote: "translucent, yellow streaks with visible exudates"
source_name: Poulin L. et al. 2014, *Plant Disease* 98(10):1423 (CGSpace abstract)

description: Formed single yellow colonies resembling *Xanthomonas* on semi-selective PSA medium.
short_quote: "Single, yellow, Xanthomonas-like colonies"

description: Produces linear water-soaked to necrotic streaks and does not enter the vascular bundles. Distinguishing the two diseases by symptoms alone is not recommended. Amber to orange exudate serves as secondary inoculum.
short_quote: "Separating the two diseases based on symptoms is not recommended."
source_name: California Dept. of Food & Agriculture, Pest Rating Proposal: *X. oryzae* pv. *oryzicola* (comment period 2026-02-25 to 04-11)

description: Typically, seedlings grow 1.5 times or more taller than normal during the seedling-raising period and then shrivel and die within 1–2 weeks. These symptoms do not all appear at once; they occur throughout the nursery period from about 10 days after sowing.
short_quote: "symptoms of growing 1.5 times or more taller than normal" (translated from Korean)

description: Seeds heavily infected by the pathogen may show stunting in the nursery and die. Therefore, judging only by elongation, the actual rate of latent infection can be more than 10 times higher.
short_quote: "actual rate of latent infection is more than 10 times higher" (translated from Korean)

category: Symptoms - seedling/root (distinguishing from etiolated seedlings: leaf angle)
description: When incidence is nearly 100%, it is hard to distinguish from ordinary etiolated seedlings. In that case, if the space between the 1st and 2nd true leaves opens 45° or more as the seedling elongates, or the 2nd and 3rd leaves do not emerge, it is bakanae.
short_quote: "the space between the 1st and 2nd true leaves opens 45° or more" (translated from Korean)

category: Symptoms - seedling/root (distinguishing from etiolated seedlings: pull test)
description: When ordinary etiolated seedlings are pulled one by one, the stem and seed come out together. In bakanae seedlings the stem and seed separate easily.
short_quote: "pulled out with the stem easily separating from the seed" (translated from Korean)

description: Rice that showed bakanae elongation in the nursery dies within 10 days after transplanting. In the paddy field, new elongation symptoms appear as plants tiller.

From 2–3 weeks after new elongation symptoms, a white layer of mycelium and spores forms on stem sheaths. Nodes may turn pale brown, and adventitious roots often emerge from the upper nodes. In severe cases the whole hill dries and dies.
short_quote: "adventitious roots emerge from the upper nodes" (translated from Korean)

category: Symptoms - whole plant (after maximum tillering, booting)
description: When disease develops after maximum tillering, depending on cultivar, leaves may turn light green and stems die without elongation symptoms. Plants may also stay tall until heading and then die without heading. Hills diseased at booting rarely head, and even if they do the grain fills poorly. Tillers are few.
short_quote: "leaves turn light green and the stem dies" (translated from Korean)

description: Disease develops best at a nursery temperature of 35 °C. It also develops at around 25 °C, but there are no symptoms at 20 °C. The optimum for fungal growth is 27–30 °C. White spores on the sheaths of plants killed after maximum tillering fly to surrounding rice flowers at flowering and lie latent in the embryo and endosperm. Spores form best at 24–32 °C and decrease sharply below 20 °C and above 35 °C.
short_quote: "disease develops best at 35℃" (translated from Korean)

description: The anamorph *F. fujikuroi* produces macroconidia, microconidia and chlamydospores. Macroconidia form on sporodochia, with 3–5 septa, 36–66 × 3–3.5 µm. Microconidia are 5–12 × 2–3 µm and form chains. In the teleomorph, perithecia are globose, 250–330 × 220–280 µm, and asci are cylindrical, 90–102 × 7–9 µm, mostly with 8 ascospores (1 septum).

A seed-borne fungal disease. It enters through roots or the crown and grows systemically inside the plant. Infected plants are abnormally tall with pale, thin leaves, few tillers, and partly filled or empty grains.
short_quote: "abnormally tall with pale, thin leaves"

description: Look for seedlings in poor condition in the nursery. Infected seedlings have lesions on the roots and may die before or just after transplanting.
short_quote: "Infected seedlings have lesions on roots"
growth_stage: Nursery bed to just after transplanting

description: Infected plants are several inches taller and thinner than healthy plants, with yellow-green or light green leaves.
short_quote: "yellowish green and pale green leaves"

description: White powdery fungal growth appears at the base or lower part of infected plants.
short_quote: "white powdery growth at the base"

description: Roots grow from the aerial nodes of the stem.
short_quote: "roots growing from above-ground nodes"

description: Not all infected plants show elongation; they may be stunted or appear normal. Early infection kills seedlings at early tillering, and late infection produces few tillers, dry leaves, and partly filled or sterile, empty grains.
short_quote: "may be stunted or appear normal"

description: Infected seed (infection rate: Nongbaek 21%, unknown cultivar 31.7%) was raised in a wet nursery. Late in the nursery some seedlings showed typical elongation, and most leaves of these elongated seedlings died shortly after transplanting. However, the remaining stems produced abundant conidia.
short_quote: "most leaves of elongated nursery seedlings die within a short time" (translated from Korean)
growth_stage: Late wet nursery to just after transplanting
source_name: Kim C.K. 1981, "Studies on the occurrence ecology of rice bakanae disease" (in Korean), listed by KoreaScience as "Korean journal of applied entomology" 20(3):146–150 (published 1981-09-01)

description: Seedlings that looked healthy in the nursery showed typical symptoms from about 2 weeks after transplanting (mid-June) and began dying with sporulation a week later. Such diseased plants increased until mid-September. The height at which conidia formed on elongated plants rose to about 40–60% of plant height in early August. Elongated plants in early July were observed to be the main inoculum for grain infection.
short_quote: "seedlings carrying the pathogen that cannot be identified visually are a problem" (translated from Korean)

description: Seedlings infected by elongation (bakanae)-type isolates show thin, long, yellowish stems and chlorotic internodes. Gibberellin (GA) produces this phenotype. This lineage produces little or no fumonisin.
short_quote: "slender, elongated and yellowish stems"

description: With the stunting-type isolate (B14), seedling and internode lengths are smaller than or similar to the uninoculated control. Withering appears from day 5 after inoculation and intensifies on days 7 and 9. On day 9 roots are heavily colonized by mycelium and root growth is strongly inhibited. No GA is detected, while fumonisins B1 and B2 are produced in large amounts.
short_quote: "no GAs but high amounts of fumonisins"

description: Of 15 field isolates obtained in 2014–2016 from Korean rice grains and air above paddies, 9 were stunting/early-withering type and 6 were elongation type. Among 151 Korean isolates, the B14-type PCR pattern accounted for 69% of rice isolates and 85% of air isolates.

category: Symptoms - whole plant (stunting type, introduced in Korea)
description: Besides the 'bakanae symptom' that elongates stems, the Korean population includes a pathotype causing a 'stem blight symptom' that stunts stem growth and then kills the plant by drying. This pathotype cannot produce gibberellin during infection and produces fumonisins and fusaric acid. In Korea the proportion of the 'blight' pathotype is far higher than the 'bakanae' pathotype.
short_quote: "stunts stem growth and then kills the plant by drying" (translated from Korean)
source_name: Newsis 2017-11-07, "IPET identifies the stem-blight mechanism of rice bakanae for the first time in the world" (citing an announcement by the Korea Institute of Planning and Evaluation for Technology in Food, Agriculture and Forestry)
source_type: Other (news media; citing a public-agency announcement)

description: Occurs only on grains. Initially the grain surface is yellow-green, so it is easy to recognize visually.
short_quote: "occurs only on grains; initially the grain surface is yellow-green" (translated from Korean)

description: Over time the hull opens slightly and a yellow-green protrusion is visible. Once powdery chlamydospores form on the surface it turns black.
short_quote: "turns black once powdery chlamydospores form" (translated from Korean)
location_in_source: Symptom description, second half of sentence 1

description: When the hull of an infected grain is removed, the inside is white and the outside dark green or black. It is easy to identify because it forms 'smut balls' (nuruk) on the panicle.
short_quote: "white inside but dark green or black outside" (translated from Korean)

description: Overwinters as sclerotia or chlamydospores. Sclerotia in the soil germinate around July–August the next year to form fruiting bodies; ascospores fly to leaf sheaths at booting and enter grains through the flowers around flowering. Low temperature with high humidity, lack of sunshine and number of rainy days have a decisive influence. There was a major outbreak in the central region in 1998.
short_quote: "environmental conditions such as low temperature and high humidity, lack of sunshine, number of rainy days" (translated from Korean)
plant_part: Leaf sheath to flower to grain

description: Early in the outbreak, round ball-shaped yellow-green protrusions (fungal spores) form on panicles and gradually turn black, so they are easy to confirm. It occurs readily when rain is frequent and humid around panicle emergence, temperatures are low at around 25 °C, and sunshine is scarce.
short_quote: "round, ball-shaped yellow-green protrusions (fungal spores)" (translated from Korean)
source_name: RDA press release 2024-08-01 "Stable rice production after the monsoon depends on disease management" (National Institute of Crop Science)

description: Occurs only on grains. Initially the grain surface is yellow-green, so it is easy to recognize visually. The pathogen enters through rice flowers at flowering.
short_quote: "initially the surface of rice grains is yellow-green" (translated from Korean)
source_name: RDA press release 2015-07-29 (reprinted on Korea Policy Briefing)

description: Velvety spore balls form on spikelets. Spore balls are orange at first and become greenish-black when mature. Individual grains are transformed into masses of spore balls.
short_quote: "initially orange and turn greenish black when mature"

description: Stage-by-stage photo captions: ① grain transformed into a velvety spore mass or yellow fruiting body ② spores grow and enclose the floral organs ③ immature spore balls are slightly flattened, smooth, yellow and enclosed by a membrane ④ spores grow and the membrane bursts ⑤ mature spores are orange, then become yellowish-green or greenish-black
short_quote: "Immature spores slightly flattened, smooth, yellow, and covered by a membrane"

description: Usually not all spikelets on a panicle are infected. Spikelets next to spore balls are often unfilled. Typically only a few grains per panicle are infected and the rest are normal.
short_quote: "spikelets neighboring smut balls are often unfilled"
location_in_source: How to identify, item 3 and last caption

description: Visible only after panicle emergence; infection can occur at flowering. Occurs at relative humidity >90% and 25–35 °C, favored by rain, high humidity and high-nitrogen soil. Damage appears in two phases: the ovary is destroyed early in flowering, and there is a second infection phase when spikelets are nearly mature.
short_quote: "visible only after panicle exsertion"
growth_stage: Infection at flowering; visible after heading
location_in_source: Why and where it occurs; Why is it important

description: Infected grains bear velvety green spore balls. Spore balls are small at first and gradually enlarge to a maximum of about 1 cm. They are visible between the glumes and enclose the floral organs.
short_quote: "grows gradually up to the size of 1 cm"
source_name: TNAU Agritech, Paddy expert system: False smut

description: As fungal growth intensifies, spore balls burst and turn orange, then yellowish-green or greenish-black. Infection usually occurs at the reproductive and grain-filling stages, and only a few grains per panicle are infected.
short_quote: "becomes orange then later yellowish-green or greenish-black"

description: Chlamydospores on spore balls are borne laterally on small sterigmata of radiating hyphae. They are globose to elliptical with warty surfaces, olive-colored, **3–5 × 4–6 µm**. Young spores are smaller, paler and almost smooth.
short_quote: "spherical to elliptical, warty, olivaceous, 3-5 x 4-6 µm"

description: Some green spore balls form 1–4 sclerotia in the center. Sclerotia overwinter in the field and produce stalked stromata in summer and autumn of the next year. Primary infection is thought to come mainly from sclerotium-derived ascospores, and secondary infection from chlamydospores.
short_quote: "develop one to four sclerotia in the center"

description: Under the light microscope, spores are round to elliptical with warty surfaces, about 3–5 µm in diameter. Under scanning electron microscopy, globose to irregularly round ornamented spores with distinct spines were seen. Spines are pointed or irregularly curved, about 200–500 nm long. The authors call these spores **conidia**.
short_quote: "diameters approximately ranging from 3 to 5 μm"
source_name: Kim K.W. & Park E.W. 2007, *Micron* 38(6):626–631 (abstract on Kyungpook National Univ. research portal)

description: Upland rice was more severely affected than paddy rice: more diseased grains per panicle, larger and heavier spore balls, and sclerotium formation on spore balls of 22.2% in upland rice versus 3.6% in paddy rice. Yellow chlamydospore balls germinated most vigorously, declining as they matured and darkened. Most diseased panicles had 1–5 infected grains, concentrated in the lower part of the panicle (near the first branch node).
short_quote: "yellow chlamydospores in the early formation stage germinate vigorously" (translated from Korean)
source_name: In M.S., Park J.S., Yu S.H. 1985, "Studies on the occurrence ecology of rice false smut" (in Korean), Research Reports of Agricultural Science (Chungnam National Univ.) 12(2):242–252

description: Overwintered sclerotia placed on the soil surface in early July germinated 81% within 19 days (May treatment: 60–70% in 41 days). They germinated at the surface to 1 cm depth at 25–30 °C, but not at 3 or 5 cm depth. Each sclerotium produced about 6 stromata, each with 50–140 perithecia. Injecting ascospores or chlamydospores into leaf sheaths at booting infected panicles. Spraying chlamydospores on seedlings was not pathogenic.
Occurs mainly on grains, but symptoms are also seen on leaf sheaths. Grains discolor yellowish-white starting from the base, gradually expanding until the whole grain is discolored.
short_quote: "grains discolor yellowish-white starting from the base" (translated from Korean)

description: In the field, panicles infected early turn pale red overall. They stand straight without bending down, and embryo development stops so the grains become empty.
short_quote: "panicles stand straight without bending down" (translated from Korean)

description: Brown rice from grains infected late is smaller than healthy rice and has brown streaks.
short_quote: "brown stripes develop" (translated from Korean)

description: When infected seed is sown, heavily infected seeds fail to germinate or rot. Seedlings from lightly infected seed have leaves that fail to unfold or sheaths that brown, grow poorly and eventually die.
short_quote: "leaf sheaths brown, growth is poor and plants eventually die" (translated from Korean)

description: Overwinters in seed and spreads to healthy seed during soaking. If the nursery is hot and humid it causes seedling rot around diseased seeds. Under unfavorable conditions it stays latent in sheaths of apparently healthy plants and enters grains when heading conditions are suitable. Major outbreaks occur when hot and humid at heading and flowering. Usually it develops readily at 10² CFU/mL of pathogen and air temperature of 20 °C or above.
short_quote: "major outbreaks when hot and humid at heading and flowering" (translated from Korean)
growth_stage: Seed soaking and seedling raising; heading and flowering

description: A short rod-shaped Gram-negative bacterium about 0.7 × 1.5–2.5 µm with 1–3 polar flagella. It forms a **light-green pigment** on King's medium B, distinguishing it from other bacteria. Its optimum growth temperature of 30–35 °C is higher than other plant pathogenic bacteria. Rice is its only natural host, and it causes seedling rot and grain rot. Seed transmission is possible.
short_quote: "forms a light-green pigment on King's medium B (KB)" (translated from Korean)

description: When infected, grains begin turning brown from where they are set just after heading, and the whole grain discolors. In severe cases panicles do not fill. It is frequent when high temperatures above 30 °C and high humidity continue around panicle emergence.
short_quote: "begins turning brown from where grains are set" (translated from Korean)
location_in_source: Body text, bacterial grain rot paragraph

description: More frequent the longer high temperatures above 30 °C continue around heading and flowering, or the more often rain of about 30 mm falls and humidity is high. It states that symptoms appear only on rice grains.
short_quote: "symptoms appear only on rice grains." (translated from Korean)
location_in_source: Body text, bacterial grain rot paragraph

description: Blighted grains on infected panicles initially have the lower third of the developing grain white to light gray, separated by a dark-brown boundary (Fig. 1).
short_quote: "white to light gray with a dark-brown margin on the bottom third"
source_name: Univ. of Arkansas Div. of Agriculture, FSA7580 "Bacterial Panicle Blight of Rice in Arkansas"(Wamishe et al.)

description: Early in infection the rachis and panicle branches stay green (Fig. 2). Grains then turn straw-colored, and by the end of the season can darken further due to secondary fungi (Fig. 3).
short_quote: "rachis or panicle branches stay green during early infection"
growth_stage: Early stage to end of season

description: Severely infected panicles stay upright because the grains do not fill (blanking) (Fig. 4). Severely infected grains have a black rotted base and the seed degenerates (Fig. 5).
short_quote: "aborted seeds with a dark basal rot"

description: On some tillers dark-brown lesions form on the flag leaf sheath (Fig. 6), and such tillers may have severe panicle damage (Fig. 7).
short_quote: "dark brown lesion on the flag leaf sheath"

description: Can be confused with wind damage (Fig. 8), water stress (Fig. 9), other environmental factors and insect damage such as stem borers.

Mainly seed-borne, but the main symptoms appear at heading. Favored by prolonged high night temperatures in summer, and long dew periods also increase disease. It can also cause seedling death, but this stage is not well known in the USA.
short_quote: "favored by extended periods of hot summer nights"

description: Linear lesions extend downward from the collar on the flag leaf sheath. They can be several inches long with reddish-brown borders and gray necrotic centers.
short_quote: "reddish-brown border and a grey, necrotic centre"
source_name: Ham J.H., Melanson R.A., Rush M.C. 2011, "*Burkholderia glumae*: next major pathogen of rice?", *Mol. Plant Pathol.* 12(4):329–339
location_in_source: Symptoms of bacterial panicle blight; Fig. 1A–B

description: One or all florets dry, and grains fail to fill or degenerate. The basal third of the floret is initially white to light gray, separated from the rest by a reddish-brown boundary, and later turns straw-colored. In severely affected fields, upright brown panicles with unfilled grains are typical.
short_quote: "Upright brown panicles"
location_in_source: Symptoms of bacterial panicle blight; Fig. 1

description: Depending on growth stage it causes grain rot, sheath rot and seedling rot. Visible symptoms appear first on the flag leaf sheath and then on the panicle. Flag-leaf-sheath symptoms predict later panicle disease. Heading and flowering are the most vulnerable stages. Unusually high temperatures (especially at night) and frequent rain at heading and flowering cause epidemics.
Gram-negative, aerobic, motile, pectolytic rods, 0.5–0.7 × 1.5–2.5 µm, with 2–4 polar flagella. Grows at 11–40 °C with an optimum of 30–35 °C; GC content about 68.2%.
short_quote: "0.5–0.7 × 1.5–2.5 µm" (figures as in original)

description: On King's B agar, toxoflavin appears as a **yellow pigment** around colonies (Fig. 1D). On CPG agar it produces visible amounts of extracellular polysaccharide (EPS). On LB + 0.2% Tween-20, lipase activity appears as an opaque iridescent halo (Fig. 1E). On pectate semi-solid medium, pectinase pitting occurs (Fig. 1F). The semi-selective medium S-PG is used for isolation and identification.
short_quote: "yellow pigment" (King's B, Fig. 1D description)

category: Culture characteristics / pathogen morphology (role of toxoflavin)
description: Toxoflavin, fervenulin and reumycin are phytotoxins, and toxoflavin is the most toxic to rice. It reduces stem and root elongation of seedlings and causes the characteristic grain rot on panicles. However, toxoflavin-deficient mutants still cause weak panicle symptoms.

*B. glumae* and *B. plantarii* were moved together from *Pseudomonas* to *Burkholderia* in 1994 and are phylogenetically close. 16S–23S rDNA spacer primers can distinguish them, and gyrB multiplex PCR distinguishes *B. glumae*, *B. gladioli* and *B. plantarii*. *B. gladioli* also causes grain rot, seedling rot and panicle blight but is isolated less often and is less virulent (estimated at about 20% of panicle blight in Louisiana and elsewhere, unpublished).

Shows the characteristic "two-tone" discoloration of grains, upright discolored panicles with green stems, and patches of upright discolored panicles in the field. Very early infection appears as water-soaked discoloration of the lower grain, and late infection as secondary fungal growth. The same pathogen also causes sheath rot.
short_quote: "characteristic two tone discoloration symptom"
source_name: LSU AgCenter, Rice Diseases Photo Galleries: Bacterial Panicle Blight
location_in_source: List of photo captions ("Characteristic Two Tone…", "Discolored Heads and Green Stems", "Early… Pathogen Infection", "Bacterial Panicle Blight Pathogen 2·3")

category: Symptoms - panicle/grain / Symptoms - sheath/stem (*B. plantarii*, Korea)
description: In September 2015, bacterial grain rot panicles showing grain degeneration and hull and grain discoloration were collected from a paddy in Suncheon. Of 66 isolates obtained on King's B medium, PCR screening yielded 2 isolates (including GRBB 15061 = KACC 18964), confirmed as *B. plantarii* by 16S rRNA, rpoD and gyrB sequences. Stem injection at tillering reproduced sheath rot, and panicle spraying at heading reproduced grain rot. The authors state this is the first report in Korea.
short_quote: "grain abortion, discoloration of the hull and grain"
source_name: Ra J.E. et al. 2016, "First report of bacterial grain rot caused by *Burkholderia plantarii* in Republic of Korea", *J. Plant Pathol.* 98(3)

description: Seedlings died in about half of the nursery boxes. Symptoms are basal yellowing and wilting of the 2nd and 3rd leaves; over time infected seedlings dry up reddish-brown and die.
short_quote: "basal chlorosis and withering of second and third leaves"
source_name: World Encyclopedia of Plant Bacterial Diseases (PlantDiseases.org), "Bacterial seedling blight / Rice" photo entry (SOURCE: K. Azegami, M. Goto)

description: Basal yellowing and wilting of the 2nd and 3rd leaves appear, and seedlings dry reddish-brown over time. Root growth is delayed so seedlings fall over easily. Another photo entry (SOURCE: H. Honma, M. Goto) describes brown, dried nursery seedlings as the same symptom.
short_quote: "Root growth is retarded and seedlings easily lodge."
source_name: PlantDiseases.org, "Bacterial seedling blight / Rice"(SOURCE: K. Azegami)

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: As an early symptom, small yellow-green spots form at the leaf base, and all leaves emerging afterwards show symptoms
short_quote: "small yellow-green spots at the leaf base" (translated from Korean)
source_name: Nongsaro pest information "Rice stripe (縞葉枯病, Stripe)"

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Young seedlings infected late in the nursery show new leaves turning yellow, rolling, drooping and dying early after transplanting
short_quote: "new leaves turn yellow, roll, droop and die" (translated from Korean)
growth_stage: Infection late in nursery bed, then early after transplanting

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: With late infection, yellowish-white lesions form on the flag leaf. Severe cases may be stunted, but plants usually look like healthy plants
short_quote: "yellowish-white lesions on the flag leaf" (translated from Korean)

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: The typical symptom is broad yellow stripes or chlorosis. Leaves fail to unfold normally, elongate and twist or droop downward
short_quote: "elongate and twist or droop downward" (translated from Korean)

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Diseased plants have fewer tillers and fail to head. Even if they head, panicles are malformed or absent, and even when panicles form, incomplete emergence is common
short_quote: "even if panicles emerge, they are malformed" (translated from Korean)

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Resistant cultivars rarely die, and large and small yellow-green lesions appear irregularly

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Symptoms begin to appear late in the nursery or around June, and are most frequent from about July 20 to early August
growth_stage: Late nursery bed to early August

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Infection occurs up to the 7-leaf stage late in the nursery, and about 50% die if infected up to the 9-leaf stage

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Susceptible japonica plants infected at the 3rd–7th leaf stage die 100%. Mortality is about 50% at the 9-leaf stage and about 20% at the 11-leaf stage, with no dead plants after the 13-leaf stage. The latent period is 7–15 days for inoculation at the 3rd–7th leaf stage and 15–30 days at the 9th–15th leaf stage
short_quote: "plants died 100% when infected" (translated from Korean)
source_name: Chung 1974, Korean Journal of Applied Entomology 13(4):181–204
location_in_source: Abstract 1 (occurrence, damage by leaf stage, latent period)

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Diseased plants are more numerous in rows near the levee and decrease toward the center. Disease is heavier in early-season cultivation

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Infected rice stems wilt, yellow and die, or if they survive they set almost no grain. Infection after the 11th true-leaf stage causes little yield loss
source_name: Nongsaro insect pest information "Small brown planthopper (striatellus)"

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Chlorotic to yellowish-white stripes, mottling and necrotic streaks form on leaves
short_quote: "chlorotic to yellowish white stripes, mottling, and necrotic streaks"
source_name: Lucid/IRRI-ACIAR-UQ Rice Doctor fact sheet "Stripe (Rice stripe virus)"

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Infected seedlings have leaves that fold, twist, wilt and droop. Plants are stunted with few tillers and panicles and may die early

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Panicles are white to brown with malformed, sterile florets and may not emerge fully. With infection after maximum tillering, chlorosis and mottling are mild and heading and grain filling may be delayed

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: The seedling to early tillering stage is most susceptible. The danger period is when viruliferous insects migrate in large numbers from overwintering winter cereals
location_in_source: Why and where it occurs / How to manage

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Chlorotic stripes and yellowing, moderate stunting and reduced vigor. In severe cases brown to gray necrotic streaks form on leaves and plants die. Panicles are few or absent, and those that form are malformed and discolored (citing Toriyama 2000)

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Slightly stunted but tiller number is normal. Pale green stripes or mottling and necrotic streaks on leaves
short_quote: "Faded green stripe or mottling and necrotic streaks"

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: *Tenuivirus* particles are thin filaments 2–2.5 nm in diameter, sometimes appearing helical, branched or panhandle-shaped. Length 200–3,000 nm (proportional to genome segment size). No envelope. 4–6 segments of negative-sense and ambisense single-stranded RNA
short_quote: "Thin, filamentous"
location_in_source: Chapter body text (virion morphology and genome description)

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: A non-structural protein (NCP) forms inclusion bodies in infected cells and is presumed to be related to symptom expression

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: RT-PCR is used to diagnose diseased plants in Korea (photos of diseased plants from Seocheon and Miryang, Fig. 1; RT-PCR detection, Fig. 2). The paper contains almost no symptom description
source_name: Lee et al. 2012, Research in Plant Disease 18(4):402–405
location_in_source: Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 captions, body text

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: States explicitly that RSV symptoms are very hard to distinguish visually from physiological disorders, and develops a precise RT-PCR diagnosis
source_name: Lee et al. 2004, Research in Plant Disease 10(1):30–33

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Adult small brown planthoppers have the sides of the back darker than the middle (the brown planthopper does not). Brown planthoppers live in groups while small brown planthoppers are scattered. Planthoppers in barley fields in April–May can be regarded as small brown planthoppers. Eggs are laid in leaf sheaths in groups of 3–10, about 400 on average
short_quote: "both sides of the back darker than the middle" (translated from Korean)
plant_part: Lower part of rice hill, leaf sheath

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Adults have macropterous (long-winged) and brachypterous (short-winged) forms. Wings are transparent and the body, mesonotum and frontal area are black to dark brown. The deep black area between the carinae of the frons is the most reliable diagnostic character. The abdomen is milky white to black. Nymphs have 5 instars, and the 5th-instar head width is 0.50–0.54 mm. Eggs are white and laid in masses of 60–260
short_quote: "deep black color ... frons ... is diagnostic"

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Transmitted in a persistent, circulative-propagative manner, mainly by the small brown planthopper. *Unkanodes sapporona*, *U. albifascia* and *Terthron albovittatum* also transmit it

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: There is transovarial transmission and transmission via sperm

scientific_name: Rice stripe virus, vector Laodelphax striatellus
description: Second-generation adult small brown planthoppers settle on young rice in the paddy field in May–June and transmit in earnest. They migrate en masse from China to the southwest coast in late May to early June
source_name: Nongsaro "Rice stripe" disease environment; Nongsaro "Small brown planthopper" ecology information
location_in_source: Disease environment sentence 4; ecology information sentence 6

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: The whole leaf turns dark green, yellowish or white spots form on the leaf surface, and the plant is severely stunted
short_quote: "the whole leaf turns dark green" (translated from Korean)
source_name: Nongsaro pest information "Rice dwarf (萎縮病, Dwarf)"

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Spots vary in size and together form stripes confined along the veins
short_quote: "stripes confined along the veins" (translated from Korean)

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Spots are also seen on the leaf sheath

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: In some cases the tips of old leaves turn yellow, and the yellowing spreads along the leaf margins
plant_part: Tips and margins of old leaves

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Tillering is usually abnormally excessive, but infection early in growth actually reduces tiller number. Root growth is severely stunted and fine roots tend to spread horizontally
short_quote: "fine roots tend to spread horizontally" (translated from Korean)
