scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Diseased rice survives to harvest in a dark green or pale green state, but fails to form panicles or has few, poorly filled grains. Dark-brown blotches form on grains, and dark-brown spots may also appear on brown rice
short_quote: "dark-brown spots also on brown rice" (translated from Korean)

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Mostly develops around late July at the end of tillering, and in early-season cultivation may develop at heading. In Korea it has occurred since 1965, with a major outbreak in 1973, expanding from the south to Chungnam, Chungbuk and Gangwon

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Viruliferous green rice leafhoppers overwinter on levees, banks and in cracks in the paddy floor, and first-generation adults fly to the nursery and infect seedlings. First-generation nymphs, second-generation adults and nymphs, and third-generation adults cause the most damage. Transmitted transovarially

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Rice dwarf currently occurs only locally in parts of the southern region, and the area affected is small
short_quote: "only locally in parts of the southern region" (translated from Korean)
source_name: Nongsaro insect pest information "Green rice leafhopper (cincticeps)"

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: White flecks and streaks form on leaves, plants are stunted and produce excessive tillers. Stunted plants fail to set seed. No galls, enations or tumors are formed
short_quote: "white flecks and streaks on leaves"

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Stunted with increased tillering. Leaves are short and dark green with fine chlorotic specks
short_quote: "dark green in color with fine chlorotic specks"

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: The characteristic symptoms are stunting and white chlorotic specks on the leaves (citing Iida et al. 1972). In Nepal, plants showing white chlorotic specks at tillering were sampled. Less than 1% of hills were diseased, and infection appeared to have occurred at early tillering
short_quote: "white chlorotic specks on foliage"
source_name: Omura et al., "Rice dwarf virus", JIRCAS TECHTARC No.21 pp.78–83
source_type: Original paper (published by international research institute)

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Polyhedral particles about 70 nm with an electron-dense core in the center. They are scattered in the cytoplasm of chlorotic tissue cells and absent from nuclei, mitochondria and chloroplasts. Confirmed by serological methods such as agar gel diffusion and latex agglutination
short_quote: "Polyhedral particles about 70 nm in diameter"

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Icosahedral particles with a distinctly angular appearance. RDV is about 70 nm in diameter with a double-shelled structure (outer: 260 P8 trimers, T=13; inner: 60 P3 dimers). The genome is 12 segments of linear dsRNA
short_quote: "distinctive angular appearance"
location_in_source: Chapter body text (virion morphology and genome description)

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Among plant reoviruses, RDV is the only one not restricted to the phloem

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: The green rice leafhopper is a green leafhopper visible to the naked eye. Together with the white-backed planthopper and small brown planthopper it is one of the most common pests of rice. Eggs are long-oval, about 1 mm long, laid in a row of 3–20 in leaf sheaths. It overwinters as 3rd–4th (or 4th) instar nymphs in weeds on south-facing levees
short_quote: "green leafhoppers can be observed with the naked eye" (translated from Korean)

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Transmitted propagatively by leafhoppers (Cicadellidae). *N. cincticeps* is most important, and *N. nigropictus*, *Recilia dorsalis* and some *Nephotettix* spp. also transmit. The latent period in the insect is about 10–20 days, after which it transmits for life. Transovarial transmission via the route of the symbiont *Candidatus* Sulcia muelleri. No sap or seed transmission

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: Persistent-propagative with transovarial transmission. Circulative period 12–25 days. Vectors are *N. cincticeps* (main), *R. dorsalis*, *N. virescens* and *N. nigropictus*

scientific_name: Rice dwarf virus, vectors Nephotettix cincticeps and others
description: The only known vector in Nepal is *N. nigropictus*. In Kathmandu it occurs from April to November, peaking in August–September
A white mycelial mat binds the panicle branches so the panicle emerges as an upright, dirty-colored cylindrical rod. No grains form on diseased panicles
short_quote: "much resembling an agarbatti or udbattta"
source_name: TNAU Agritech Portal, Expert System for Paddy "Udbatta disease"

description: Before heading, white mycelium and conidia form narrow streaks along the veins of the flag leaf
Grayish-white mycelium grows on young leaves of infected seedlings, suggesting that infection occurs during germination

Externally seed-borne and systemic. Since diseased panicles do not set grain, infected seed is of low importance as inoculum. Alternative hosts are *Isachne elegans*, *Cynodon dactylon*, *Pennisetum* sp. and *Eragrostis tenuifolia*
Favored by high temperature and humidity and by the maximum tillering to panicle initiation stage. Disease is low with very early or very late sowing

A minor disease present only in some areas (mainly highlands). It has no noticeable effect on growth or appearance, so diseased plants cannot be identified until heading. Heading is similar to or slightly earlier than healthy plants

Instead of a normal panicle, a rod-like structure ("agarbathi") emerges from the flag leaf. Masses of mycelium and spores bind the florets to the axis, forming a hard crust. Usually all tillers of a hill are infected, showing that infection is systemic
short_quote: "rod-shaped structure"

description: Not distinguishable until the flag leaf stage. Diseased panicles emerge as upright, grayish-white cylindrical structures resembling an incense stick (agarbatti), replacing the normal panicle. Diseased plants have all panicles infected, and even one infected panicle means complete yield loss for that panicle
short_quote: "erect, grayish-white, cylindrical structures"
source_name: Vineeth et al. 2025, Mysore J. Agric. Sci. 59(3):428–444

description: Common in low hill areas of Bihar, Odisha, Maharashtra and Karnataka, India, where soil temperatures are high (about 28 °C) and humid. In 2018, disease incidence reached up to 50% in cultivar Tunga in Karnataka and 10–30% in BR2655 and MTU 1001. In 2022–24 it was severe in major cultivars such as Jyothi and Jaya

The pathogen was isolated from diseased panicles by the spore drop method. On PDA, colonies are raised and cottony with a leathery, waxy texture. Identified by colony characteristics and conidia (named *E. japonica*)
short_quote: "elevated, fluffy, with a leathery and waxy texture"
location_in_source: Results and Discussion – Isolation of the Pathogen

description: (Forage grasses, not rice) The fungus covers the inflorescence and prevents it from unfolding, giving a mummified appearance. Mature stromata are grayish-white to black depending on maturity and host, and grayish-black sclerotium-like structures 1–2 mm in diameter may form on the panicle
short_quote: "Sclerotia-like structures, grayish black and 1–2 mm"

description: (Japanese grass isolates) Conidiophores arise in a palisade on the stroma, and conidia form from slender phialides at the tips. Conidia are colorless, needle-shaped, aseptate, 8.8–27.9 × 0.9–2.7 µm, with one nucleus (DAPI staining). The abstract gives 10–25 × 0.5–1 µm. The sexual stage was not observed in nature
short_quote: "colorless, needle-shaped, non-septate"

description: (Grasses) Mycelium grows epiphytically on the leaf surface forming white leaf streaks. SEM shows hyphal strands bearing masses of conidia extending epiphytically on the leaf surface, with no tissue penetration observed
There are no reports on rice in Japan. Since there is no difference in the original descriptions of *E. oryzae* and *E. japonica*, *E. japonica* is adopted by priority
Preferred name *Balansia oryzae-sativae* Hashioka. Synonyms *Balansia oryzae*, *Ephelis oryzae* Sydow. English names black choke, false ergot, incense rod, udbatta

Mature stromata form on the inflorescence and contain perithecia. Immature stromata have cup- to cushion-shaped black conidiomata. Conidia are colorless, filiform to needle-shaped, about 18–22 × 1.5 µm. With age the inflorescence darkens and pseudosclerotia form, giving a mummified look **(search snippet; original returned 403 and is Unconfirmed; host and region also Unconfirmed)**
Describes the sexual stage as *Balansia oryzae-sativae*, with the micrograph caption reading "*Ephelis oryzae*". No description of stroma, sclerotium or conidial sizes
From seedling to flag leaf stage the main symptom is leaf chlorosis. Plants become deformed, and distinct white patches or splash-pattern spots form at the base of young leaves
short_quote: "speckles in a splash pattern"

description: Necrotic brown stains form on leaves and sheaths and gradually darken, and parts of the upper internodes turn dark brown. Leaf sheaths become deformed
The bases of young leaves twist, and **lower nodes may swell and branch irregularly**
short_quote: "lower nodes can become swollen with irregular branching"

description: Depending on severity, chlorotic parts, tillers or whole hills wilt and die, appearing light brown. In severe cases the whole crop is affected and dark-brown patches form in the field (usually after panicle initiation)

After heading, panicles are usually crinkled, and glumes, especially at the base, are empty and shriveled. Panicles and flag leaves twist and distort. Panicles are completely enclosed in a swollen sheath, emerge only partly, or are sterile
short_quote: "enclosed within a swollen sheath"

description: At harvest, stems carrying healthy panicles lodge, while infected stems carrying empty panicles stand upright (citing Cox & Rahman 1980)
short_quote: "remain erect"

description: Early on, nematodes hide inside the leaf sheath and are hard to detect. At the vegetative stage there is chlorosis, deformation, white splash spots at the base of young leaves, brown necrosis on leaves and sheaths, twisting of leaf bases, sheath deformation, swollen lower nodes and irregular branching. Later, dark-brown patches, partial heading, panicles inside swollen sheaths, sterility, empty panicles and upright stems at harvest appear

Early symptoms are hard to recognize. At about 2 months, white patches or splash patterns of dots and dashes at the leaf base, mosaic-like discoloration, chlorosis, and white streaks on young leaves and sheaths appear. The most typical and distinct symptoms are seen at heading. By severity and timing it is divided into **thor ufra (swollen ufra)** and **pucca ufra (ripe ufra)**, and there is also a three-grade system of ufra-I, II and III
short_quote: "thor ufra" / "pucca ufra"
growth_stage: About 2 months after transplanting to heading
source_name: Das D. 2024, "Ufra – The Deeply Mysterious Disease", Indian J. Nematology 53(Spl):49–60

description: In swollen ufra the panicle remains enclosed in the sheath; in ripe ufra the panicle emerges but grains set only partly at the tip **(search snippet; original Unconfirmed due to DNS error)**

Emerging and already emerged leaves show mosaic or chlorotic discoloration, yellowish or pale green splash patterns on leaves and sheaths, brown to dark-brown spots on leaves, and corrugated leaf margins. With early infection panicles fail to emerge
short_quote: "mosaic or chlorotic discolouration"

description: In irrigated and deepwater rice in Bangladesh, symptoms usually appear in late July to August. Symptoms appear within 1 week in young plants and within 10–15 days in plants around flowering

First observed about 2 months after transplanting. Early heading is the best time for surveys, and the most distinct symptoms appear on panicles (Ou 1985). Low-density infections are hard to find visually

15 females (Joydevpur, Bangladesh): L=0.8–1.20 mm, a=50–62, b=6–9, c=18–24, V=78–80, stylet 10–11 µm. 10 males: L=0.7–1.18 mm, spicules 16–21 µm, stylet 10 µm. Juveniles L=0.5–0.7 mm, stylet 8–10 µm. description: The female body is slender, nearly straight or slightly curved ventrally when relaxed. The lip region is unannulated, low and flat. The lateral field is 1/4 or less of body width with 4 lateral lines. The stylet is moderately developed, with the conus about 45% of stylet length and small distinct knobs (about 2 µm). The posterior oesophageal bulb is clavate (27–34 µm) and slightly overlaps the intestine. The ovary extends forward with oocytes in 1 row (rarely 2). The post-uterine sac is 2.0–2.5 times the body width at the vulva. **The tail is conoid, 5.2–5.4 times the anal body width, with a sharp tip that looks like a mucro.** Males are as numerous as females and the bursa extends nearly to the tail tip

description: Distinguished from other species by tail shape and size, the relative lengths of stylet and post-uterine sac, and the number of lateral lines (Fortuner 1982). *Aphelenchoides besseyi* (white tip nematode) has oesophageal glands extensively overlapping the anterior intestine, 3–4 processes at the tail tip, males without a bursa, and oocytes in 2–4 rows in the female ovary. In contrast, *D. angustus* males have a bursa and female oocytes are mainly in 1 row
